implementation_notes: C++11 standardized the pre-C++11 idiom as a container member: std::vector, std::deque and std::basic_string declare shrink_to_fit(), documented as a non-binding request to reduce capacity() to size() - 'It depends on the implementation whether the request is fulfilled'. It is at most linear in size and invalidates every iterator, pointer and reference (end() included) whenever it reallocates, so it belongs at a quiescent point after the shrink phase (erase-remove, filtering) with data()/iterators re-acquired afterwards. Choose it when the container stays the same type and must remain growable; choose the swap variant when the capacity must really fall or when the toolchain predates C++11.
code_sketch:
std::vector<Record> v = load_all();              // capacity ~100'000
v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), stale), v.end());
v.shrink_to_fit();                               // non-binding: capacity may fall to size()
Record *first = v.data();                        // re-acquire: the buffer may have moved
pitfalls: shrink_to_fit() is a non-binding request: an implementation may ignore it or stop above size(), so a memory budget cannot rest on it - the swap trick is the binding form.

Reallocation invalidates all iterators, pointers and references, end() included: iterating while trimming, or holding an iterator, pointer or string_view into the container across the call, is a dangling-access bug.
Since C++11 the call is undefined behaviour unless T is MoveInsertable, and trimming in a loop after each removal turns amortized O(1) appends into repeated O(n) copies.
sources: cppreference, std::vector<T,Allocator>::shrink_to_fit - 'Requests the removal of unused capacity. It is a non-binding request to reduce capacity() to size(). It depends on the implementation whether the request is fulfilled'; 'If reallocation occurs, all iterators (including the end() iterator) and all references to the elements are invalidated'; complexity at most linear: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/shrink_to_fit

variants.name: swap with a right-sized temporary (pre-C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: The original idiom (Meyers' 'swap-to-fit'): build a temporary holding exactly the survivors and swap its buffer with the container's, letting the temporary destroy the old storage when it goes out of scope. Use the range constructor - std::vector<T>(v.begin(), v.end()).swap(v) - rather than the copy constructor, because the copy form is only capacity-optimal if the implementation guarantees it (the originating chapter's own footnote questions that guarantee, and for reference-counted string implementations only the range form is reliable). Choose this variant when the toolchain predates C++11 or when the capacity must actually be released, since it is not a non-binding request; the price is an unconditional full copy plus a second allocation of the survivors' size.
pitfalls: The copy-constructor form std::vector<int>(v).swap(v) is optimal only under a guarantee the chapter itself questions - the range-constructor form is the reliable one.
The swap is cheap but the copy is not: every element is copied and both buffers are live at once, so trimming under memory pressure can fail where a no-copy variant would not.
swap() requires same type and equal allocators; with unequal allocators the swap is undefined, which turns 'shrink the buffer' into memory corruption rather than an error.
sources: More C++ Idioms (Wikibooks), 'Shrink-to-fit' - the sample std::vector<int>(v).swap(v) ('v is swapped with its temporary copy, which is capacity optimal'), its footnote questioning that the copy constructor is guaranteed to allocate just enough, and the recommended 'range constructor' form std::vector<int>(v.begin(), v.end()).swap(v): https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/More_C%2B%2B_Idioms/Shrink-to-fit
